heuristics.name: random-mapping idealization
heuristics.statement: For collision purposes the R-adding iteration on the affine x high-bit partition behaves like a uniform random mapping on the r group points: walk iterates are modeled as independent uniform draws until the first repeat.
heuristics.support: Standard r-adding-walk analysis (Teske ANTS 1998; Brent-Pollard) finds only small-constant deviations from the idealization for R >= 20 partitions; the packaged toy experiment runs the identical construction end-to-end and measures 1.40x the idealized steps-to-solve. The claim does not rely on any exact external constant.
heuristics.limitations: Declared heuristic, not a theorem. A toy run at r = 2089 does not bind the constant at r ~ 2^256; the claim therefore does not assert the idealization but bounds against its failure.
heuristics.extrapolation: The bound survives a degradation of the collision exponent by a factor of 2.09: the submitted budget k = 46*2^123 gives exponent 1.0332 vs the 0.4943 required for success 0.39.

limitations: Analytic construction; no full-size execution or independent qualification.
Success rests on the single disclosed heuristic M1 with a quantified 2.09x margin; if real r-adding walks deviate worse than that, the success bound fails and so does the claim.
Instruction bounds are analytical upper bounds, not Callgrind measurements of a P-256 kernel.
The negation map was deliberately not used: its fruitless-cycle analysis could not be reproduced compactly enough to satisfy the evidence policy, so the claim pays ~0.64 bits of score to remove it.
This is a generic best-known-style accounting, not a novelty or practical-break claim.
